chapter: Caravan, Perdido and the first tunes
title: Writing Caravan and selling it to Irving Mills for $25
summary: At the Los Angeles Cotton Club an MGM music director praised his trombone tone and Caravan; Mills paid him $25 outright and later gave him a percentage.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: When was the first composition you wrote with Duke?
After you were with Duke, what was the first composition you wrote?

Well, the first one was Caravan, which just happened to be -- we was at the Cotton Club here in Los Angeles, and Duke invited a famous director from MGM, the music director -- oh, I can never recall people's names -- but anyhow, he invited him to come to the Cotton Club, after we get through and they closed the place, and this group -- we were going to give him like a small concert or something. But before the concert, I used to go there in the front and play the band and play anything Spanish on my trombone, and I didn't know he was there already; I thought he was going to come over after the place was closed, but he was already in the Cotton Club.

So after the concert, we played everything; we played Concerto for Barney, Concerto for Cootie, concerto for so and so -- everyone -- he threw everything he had in the book at us, and he made me play Caravan, so I played Caravan, and when we finished with the concert -- we usually go for inter-

mission, we go in the kitchen or in the back of the stage to talk or eat something, and Duke Ellington came back there and he said, 'Well, I'm gonna tell you something. I hope your heads don't get big from what I tell you, but so and so -- that's the conductor -- he said the thing that he went for, was first, the tone and then your trombone. He said, that was the first tone of a trombone I ever heard in my life. And then besides, for Caravan.
Newman was his name, wasn't it?
Newman was his name, wasn't it?

No, no. It was not Newman. So he went for my tone on the trombone, and for the tune, 'Caravan.' So in the next two or three weeks, he came to the Cotton Club with all kind of contraptions and everything about 'Caravan.' You know how much he gave me?
Twenty-five dollars. Until later on, I guess his heart got so -- later in the years, later in years, he decided to give me a percentage on the composition. Because I sold it outright, you know?
